# META-INSIGHTS — about the optimization PROCESS itself (this run)

Not about the capability — about HOW this run is searching for it: which strategies/edit classes/algorithms are helping vs stalling, and what to try next iteration. Update at the end of the run at minimum; sooner if a plateau or a clear strategy shift is worth recording now. Structure each addition as:

    ## Iteration <id> (or 'run so far')
    - Strategy tried, and whether it moved val (cite LEDGER rows):
    - Plateau/stall signal, if any, and the lever switched to:
    - What to try next iteration:

## Iteration cand_0001 (first of the run; empty seed)

- **Strategy tried:** an empty seed is not "iteration 1 of a hill climb", it is a cold start, so I
  did not hunt for one big lever. I clustered **all 22** failures first, then shipped one edit per
  cluster with a different lever type each (CONTRACT, STRUCTURE-ordering, STRUCTURE-code,
  DECISION-rule, KNOWLEDGE-fact, KNOWLEDGE-idiom). No LEDGER rows exist yet to cite.
- **The process step that paid off most was cheap and non-obvious: reading the adapter read-only
  before writing a word of prose.** It revealed that an *empty* `prompt.md` means "no system
  message" (not a default), that the built-in template carries the "file exists ⇒ done" line, that
  only the first code block is executed, and that the preview is `header=0`. Four of the eight
  shipped edits exist only because of that read. Recommend every cold-start iteration do this first.
- **Counting beat reasoning.** Two tallies decided the candidate's shape: formula-writers 0/13 vs
  literal-writers 18/27, and 39-of-40 never-verified. Both took minutes to compute from the traces
  and are far stronger evidence than reading any single trace closely. Cheap aggregate counts over
  all trajectories, before deep-reading any of them.
- **The highest-value process step was regression-testing my own prose as code.** The audit snippet
  is the only edit that tells the agent to go back and change a file it may already have written
  correctly — so I extracted it verbatim from the written file and *ran* it against real workbooks
  for 13 tasks (8 passing, 5 failing). That found **two real bugs I would otherwise have shipped**:
  unbounded printing (1280 lines), and a classifier that swept legitimately-blank cells into
  `MUST-FIX`, false-alarming on exactly the 5 fragile passing tasks. **Generalizable rule: if a
  prompt edit contains executable code, execute it against gold before shipping — do not review it
  by reading.**
- **A self-audit against gold caught an over-strong rule.** I had written "empty is never an answer";
  checking gold blankness across the 18 passing tasks showed 5 of them have legitimately blank gold
  (382-10 is 79% blank). The SAFE test is much sharper when run as a *query against the passing
  tasks' gold* than as introspection about blast radius.
- **Subagents:** read-only `Explore` agents per trajectory group for clustering, merged into one
  candidate. Useful for breadth. One of my own hypotheses was refuted by a subagent's evidence,
  which changed shipped wording — so state hypotheses explicitly in the delegation prompt and ask
  for disconfirmation, not confirmation.
- **Plateau signal:** none possible yet.
- **What to try next iteration:** (a) read cand_0001's RESULT before anything else — with 8 edits
  shipped together, a rejection will not say which one hurt, so if it regresses, bisect by lever
  (drop the audit snippet first; it has the largest behavioural blast radius) rather than rewriting.
  (b) If it lands, the remaining mass is *semantic* misreading of the instruction (unit of
  aggregation, which row set) — a different lever class from anything shipped here, which was all
  contract/mechanics. (c) Keep the "run the prose" discipline; it is the only step this iteration
  that found defects nothing else would have.
- **Cost note for the run:** the breadth-first approach used one iteration to cover 8 clusters. If
  the RESULT is a clean accept, prefer breadth again; if it is a rejection with a small `broke={}`
  set, the run will have paid a whole iteration to learn one bad edit — in that case switch to
  2–3 edits per iteration so attribution is possible.

## Iteration 2 (cand_0002) — the search process, revised by what iteration 1 actually taught

- **The single highest-value technique in this run: EXECUTE the prose you are about to ship.**
  cand_0001 flagged this as a discipline to keep; it paid twice this iteration. Running its own
  audit snippet verbatim over all 40 tasks found (a) a `KeyError` crash on 2 passing tasks and
  (b) a `datetime` → `FORMULA-OBJECT` misclassification that false-alarmed on 3 more **passing**
  tasks. Neither is visible by reading. **A prompt that contains code is partly testable, so the
  "prompt edits can't be unit-tested" excuse is only half true — test the testable half.** The
  reusable harness: build a "perfect answer" workbook (golden values as literals on top of the real
  input), run the snippet on every task, require **zero false alarms on the passing set**.
- **cand_0001's own forward plan was wrong, and checking beat trusting it.** It handed over two
  confident next steps — an ARGB/formatting rule for 267-18 and a "restate the unit of aggregation"
  step for the semantic cluster. Both were refuted in 20 minutes of trace reading: 267-18 reads the
  correct colour and fails on an erased input formula; 43436 already aggregates correctly and fails
  on one comparison operator. **Lesson for the handover format: a prior iteration's "focus next
  iteration" is a hypothesis written without its RESULT, so re-derive the cluster from this
  iteration's traces before spending an edit on it.** The JOURNAL's value is its refutations and
  RESULT lines, not its forecasts.
- **Scorer feedback strings are precise cluster labels — read them as diagnostics, not summaries.**
  *"N cell(s) hold a number HIGHER than expected"* with full coverage and right types ⇒ a boundary
  operator, not a logic error. *"M cell(s) were CHANGED although the expected value is the cell's
  own original input"* ⇒ the workbook's worked example was overridden. *"the answer cells hold
  FORMULAS"* ⇒ check whether the *input* put them there before assuming the agent wrote them. Each
  of these pointed at the root cause faster than reading the trace did.
- **`init` vs `golden` across ALL tasks is the sharpest SAFE test available** (cand_0001 found this
  for blank-gold; it generalizes). One scripted sweep answered every blast-radius question this
  iteration in a form I could quote: *7 of 40 tasks have an input formula in range; 20 have
  pre-filled cells, 13 of which gold keeps and 7 of which gold changes.* Introspecting about blast
  radius produces adjectives; querying the gold produces counts and task ids. **Do the sweep first,
  before drafting any edit — it also tells you which edits are pointless.**
- **Breadth was cheap here because the failures were genuinely independent.** 4 failures, 4 distinct
  root causes, no shared wording — so 6 edits carried near-zero mutual interference risk. Contrast
  with cand_0001's 8 edits on 22 overlapping failures. **Heuristic: breadth is safe in proportion to
  how disjoint the root causes are, not to how many tasks are failing.** Attribution is still the
  cost — if this candidate is rejected, bisect by dropping the two edits with real behavioural reach
  (Rule 2b's geometry rule, and the `ERASED` audit) before touching the three knowledge-only edits.
- **Plateau signal:** none — 1 prior RESULT, +0.450. But headroom is now ~0.10 on 4 tasks, so from
  here the run is defending a high score rather than climbing. **With 3 iterations left after this
  one, the dominant risk flips from "not enough gain" to "one speculative edit sinks a good
  candidate."** Subsequent iterations should shrink batch size and raise the verification bar, not
  reach for new clusters that do not exist in the traces.
- **What to try next iteration:** (a) read the RESULT first, and for any still-failing task ask
  *did the agent run the new step at all?* — a skipped step means promote it from prose into the
  pasteable snippet (code enforcement is what worked in cand_0001), not more emphasis. (b) If all 4
  landed, resist inventing clusters: spend the iteration hardening the audit's blank-vs-erased
  judgement and 402-43's latent round-trip fragility, both of which are places a *future* edit
  regresses. (c) Subagents were not used this iteration — 4 failures fit one context and the
  decisive evidence was one uniform sweep. **Fan-out earns its cost when failures are many and
  heterogeneous; with a handful of failures, delegation adds summarization loss for no coverage gain.**
